# Selection — TRD §15 row 15: interrupted-rotation and downgrade behaviour

**Status:** selected, and folded into the TRD. **Date:** 2026-08-20
**Closes:** TRD §15 row 15, and the atomic-replace half [row 14](./row-14-recovery-code.md) §5 deferred ·
**Scope of:** review 3b (protocol)
**Constrained by:** TRD §13.7, §13.5, §14.4, §11.2 test 11 · PRD §6.10 · **Stage:** [sequencing.md](../sequencing.md) §3.1
**Vectors:** [`test/vectors/transition.json`](../../test/vectors/transition.json), generated by
[`scripts/generate-transition-vectors.mjs`](../../scripts/generate-transition-vectors.mjs)
**Companions:** [row 6](./row-6-antireplay-retention.md) selects the outbound rule this extends by one case and
leaves one gap in; [row 7](./row-7-checkpoint.md) supplies the cadence rule an interruption violates;
[row 3](./row-3-record-format.md) supplies the finding about an editable `kind`;
[row 10](./row-10-portable-package.md) supplies the rule against binding a derivable fact twice;
[row 12](./row-12-account-credential.md) supplies the shape of an isolating negative for a field read twice.
**Amended by:** [`S0-2`](../review/remediation/S0-2/README.md) (2026-08-27) — three changes. The `replace-recovery` payload parts become byte-exact and mirror `rotate`'s shape;
`applying` becomes a durable eight-step record rather than a named state; and the generation-drop gate gains a
fourth clause for retained-checkpoint openers (TRD §§13.7–13.8).
**Amended by:** [`S0-5`](../review/remediation/S0-5/README.md) (2026-08-27) — the generation-application record's checkpoint step means **semantically admitted**, not merely
produced. A signed manifest alone no longer discharges it (TRD §7.6, `S0-2` Stage A).
**Amended by:** [`S0-6`](../review/remediation/S0-6/README.md) (2026-08-27) — `retire` commits terminal lineage, and hosted deletion now waits on a durable
`TerminalHandoff` from a verified-current receiver rather than on an elapsed window (TRD §14.4).
**Amended by:** [`S0-7`](../review/remediation/S0-7/README.md) (2026-08-27) — §8's _product downgrade_ cell is
narrowed. Binding `kind` closes the `rotate`/`retire` pair and does not close lapse, which this grammar cannot
express; lapse is carried by TRD §14.7's retention machine and the three kinds stay three.

---

## The selection

```
One intent-and-outcome protocol, at three kinds

  Intent  = LP("done/transition/v1") || LP(dec v) || LP(kind)
            || LP(workspace_id) || LP(lineage_id) || LP(dec parent_epoch)
            || LP(dec target) || LP(hex payload_digest)
  sig     = Ed25519( the requesting device's signing credential ; Intent )
  id      = SHA-256(Intent)

    kind  'rotate'            target = the generation being rotated to
          'replace-recovery'  target = the replacement counter
          'retire'            target = the terminal epoch

    payload_digest  the kind's own parts, sorted by name under
                    LP("done/transition-payload/v1")

      rotate            cutoff, excluded, recovery-wrap, wraps
      replace-recovery  counter, new-recovery-public-key, recovery-envelope,
                        root-commitment, successor-generation, wraps
      retire            reason, terminal-head

      Every wrap and envelope value is the EXACT bytes, tag included --
      never a count, an id list or a generation number. A digest over
      WHICH generations were rewrapped, and not over what they were
      rewrapped TO, cannot make atomicity mean one exact set won.

      successor-generation is dec g+1, or the explicit string
      'none-lost-not-copied'. Replacement offered as the answer to an
      EXPOSED code must rotate: resealing leaves K_g unchanged.

  No from_gen: the epoch already binds the current generation.

  Persisted before the first network byte. The service commits at most one
  intent per (lineage_id, kind, target).

Outcome — the only thing that licenses discarding a live content key

  Outcome = LP("done/transition-out/v1") || LP(dec v) || LP(kind)
            || LP(workspace_id) || LP(lineage_id) || LP(dec target)
            || LP(dec epoch) || LP(hex committed_id)
  sig     = Ed25519( the lineage authorization key of `epoch` ; Outcome )

  No state flag: whether you won is committed_id == your id.
  No nonce: (lineage, kind, target) names a pair reached once.

The three-way rule

  silence                        wait, resubmit the identical bytes
  outcome, committed_id == id    committed — apply
  outcome, committed_id != id    superseded — discard, rebuild against the
                                 new epoch. NOT resubmit.

  Everything that is not a verified outcome is silence. A timeout is
  silence, a reset is silence, an unsigned error body is silence.

Local order

  pending persisted --submit--> pending --outcome(mine)--> applying --> settled
                                        --outcome(other)--> stale --> rebuild

  No content under the target generation before a committed outcome.
  None under the previous generation after it.
  applying is a DURABLE RECORD, not a label. Eight ordered idempotent steps:
    1 outcome verified   2 successor opener installed   3 old objects classified
    4 work covered under g+1   5 ACTIVE MARKER ADVANCED -- the commit point
    6 successor checkpoint admitted, local content trimmed
    7 old openers retired   8 apply record discharged
  Restart resumes at the recorded step. 1-4 reversible; 5 is not.
  Device lock and replace-recovery apply through this same machine.

  The previous generation is retained until settled AND a checkpoint under
  the new one is admitted AND the local trim holds a state record under it
  AND every retained checkpoint still sealed under it has a surviving
  authorized opener. The fourth clause is what keeps the second-newest
  checkpoint openable; the first three only permit the drop.

                LP(s) = uint16be(byteLength(utf8 s)) || utf8 s
```

Everything below is why, and what it cost.

---

## 1. The row's subject is a class, and §11.2 test 11 already listed it

Test 11 reads as five unrelated failures: "Unsupported PRF, interrupted enrollment, duplicate recovery,
concurrent authorization changes and a half-completed account deletion fail closed without silently changing
the confidentiality promise." Written out, they are one shape.

| Interruption                     | The completed transition it can be mistaken for    |
| -------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------- |
| A rotation that did not settle   | No rotation was needed                             |
| A revocation that did not settle | The credential is still authorized                 |
| A deliberate downgrade           | **Account deletion** (PRD §6.10 says exactly this) |
| A recovery replacement           | Neither envelope replaced, or **both live**        |
| An enrollment                    | Enrolled                                           |

**So _fail closed_ is not five properties. It is one: the intermediate state must be representable, distinguishable
and resolvable, and must never be a valid representation of an endpoint.** Every item in the table is an
intermediate state that reads as a _lesser_ endpoint — one with fewer guarantees — which is why the failure mode
is silent rather than loud. Nothing errors; something is simply weaker than it was believed to be.

**That is why there is one protocol rather than three.** Rotation, recovery replacement and retirement have
different payloads and the same problem, and giving each its own message shape would mean arguing the same
argument three times and getting it right two of them.

---

## 2. PRD §6.10's sentence is a binding requirement, not interface guidance

> **Deliberate downgrade is the same mechanism**, and it must not silently become account deletion.

Read in the PRD this is a warning about a screen. Written as bytes it is a field. A `rotate` and a `retire`
intent are **the same eight fields** — same workspace, same lineage, same parent epoch, same target — differing
in `kind` and in the payload that `kind` selects. **An unbound `kind` is a way to submit one and commit the
other**, and the difference between them is the entire distinction §13.5 draws between a _live_ lineage and a
_retired_ one.

**Row 3 found this exact thing about a `StoredRecord`'s `kind`**, where an editable one lets the store delete its
own history through its own trim path. This is that finding at a third object, and the consequence is one level
larger: there, a store loses its history; here, a lapse retires a lineage that PRD §6.10 says stays live.

The vectors publish the two intents side by side, with the byte at which their messages first diverge, because
the sentence is easier to believe as a diff than as a claim.

**What that diff reaches, and where this row overclaimed it** (`S0-7`). It proves a `rotate` cannot commit as a
`retire`, which is real and is the pair PRD §6.10's sentence is about at the protocol layer. It does **not**
reach lapse, because **there is no lapse intent to diverge from**: the grammar has three kinds and none of them
carries a payment state, a synchronization stop or a retention deadline. Read as _product downgrade is closed_,
this row was standing a true local statement in for a total one — the shape row 4's carrier registry was caught
in — and an implementation reading it would have had to misuse `rotate`, use `retire` and destroy the
live-lineage guarantee, or invent state the register calls common and never defined. **TRD §14.7 defines that
state**, on a second axis and under a signer that is not the lineage key, and this row's contribution is
unchanged: the ordering is the fail-closed property, and `kind` has a negative.

---

## 3. Row 6's rule extends by one case, and the third case is the dangerous one

Row 6 selected the outbound rule for envelope positions: **re-mint only on a definite refusal, never on silence.**
Two states, because an envelope is one position and a refusal means the service never took it.

A transition has three, and the third exists only because it carries an **exclusion set**:

| What the client sees                  | What it means                           | What it does                                |
| ------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------- |
| Silence                               | Unknown — committed, in flight, or lost | **Wait**, then resubmit the identical bytes |
| Outcome, `committed_id` == its own id | It won                                  | Apply                                       |
| Outcome, `committed_id` != its own id | Another device won the race             | **Discard and rebuild**, never resubmit     |

**Resubmitting on the third case would be wrong, and the reason is not obvious.** The intent's exclusion set was
computed against `parent_epoch`. The winner excluded a _different_ credential. Resubmitting the same bytes at the
next generation would exclude someone the workspace has already decided to keep and keep someone it has already
decided to exclude — a revocation that revokes the wrong person, produced by a retry that looks correct.

**So the second and third cases are opposite instructions, and only a signed outcome distinguishes them.**

---

## 4. A definite refusal licenses discarding a live key, so it has to be authenticated

**This is the gap row 6 left, and it is left by the rule rather than by an oversight.** Row 6 wrote _a definite
refusal is the only thing that licenses a re-mint; silence is not one_ — and said nothing about where a definite
refusal comes from. For an envelope the consequence of a forged one is bounded: the client re-mints at the same
position, which row 6's own equivocation analysis already covers.

**Here the consequence is a discarded content key.** A fabricated _superseded_ outcome makes an honest client
throw away `K_(g+1)` and every wrap it made, and rebuild against an epoch the attacker chose the timing of.
Repeated, it is a rotation that never completes — so a credential the owner is trying to exclude stays able to
read, indefinitely, while the interface reports a rotation in progress. **That is §11.2 test 11's confidentiality
promise changing silently, achieved with no key material at all.**

**So the outcome is signed by the lineage authorization key, and everything unsigned is silence.** Not an error,
not a refusal, not a retryable failure — _silence_, which the client waits through. A relay that can withhold an
outcome can also fabricate one, and §7.2's content-blindness means it is not trusted with anything else either.

**One consequence worth stating because it looks like a bug:** a client that cannot reach the service after
submitting is stuck holding a pending intent, and it must stay stuck. That is the fail-closed direction. The
alternative — timing out and rebuilding — is precisely the attack above, performed by the network instead of by
an attacker.

---

## 5. What the commit is, and why neither half may precede it

Rotation does two things: it changes the content key, and it excludes a credential. Interrupted between them,
each order fails differently.

| Order                | The window it opens                                                                                                   |
| -------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Exclude, then re-key | The credential is excluded and new content is still under the generation it holds. **Fails open**                     |
| Re-key, then exclude | The credential is still authorized and cannot read new content. Fails closed, at the cost of writes it can still make |

**So neither is selected: the atomic commit is one transition point and neither half may precede it.** §13.7
already says the service "atomically commits and signs that package"; what this row adds is the client-side rule
that makes the atomicity mean anything — **the local writer switches generation on observing a verified committed
outcome, and only then.** No content under the target generation before it, none under the previous generation
after it.

**The crash case is what the pending record is for.** A client that committed and died before switching restarts
holding a pending intent, resubmits it, and gets back the outcome naming its own id — because the service commits
at most one intent per `(lineage_id, kind, target)` and a retry is byte-identical. **Row 13 named its impossible
state the same way**; this row's are three:

- **A committed transition with no local record that it was intended** — prevented by persisting before the first
  network byte.
- **Content sealed under a generation no committed epoch names** — prevented by not writing under the target
  before settling.
- **A dropped generation with no checkpoint under its successor** — §6.

---

## 6. A retry has to be the same bytes, and that is a sorting problem

The idempotency key is `SHA-256` of the intent message, so _resubmit the identical bytes_ is only safe if
rebuilding the intent produces identical bytes. The wraps are a map, the exclusion set is a set, and the cutoff is
row 5's head vector — **three unordered collections, and a map in insertion order would make a retry a second,
different transition.**

**Row 7 found this at the head vector and called the sort load-bearing rather than tidy.** It is the same finding
one object along, and the consequence here is sharper: there, two devices checkpointing the same state would
disagree and it would read as a corrupt manifest; here, a client retrying after a lost response would submit an
intent the service has never seen, at a generation it has already committed.

The generator builds every payload twice, from inputs in a different order, and fails if the digests disagree.

---

## 7. The retention condition an interruption is exactly what violates

Row 7 selected a cadence rule that is easy to read as bookkeeping: **a rotation must produce a checkpoint under
the new generation before the old one may be dropped**, or tidying up destroys the recovery path.

**An interrupted rotation is the case that breaks it**, because the obvious implementation clears
`rotation_owed` when the epoch commits — which is before the checkpoint exists. So the condition is three, not
one, and all three must hold before the previous generation is dropped:

1. The outcome is committed.
2. A checkpoint under the new generation is admitted (row 7).
3. The local trim holds a state record under the new generation (§6.1).

**Dropping on fewer than three is found at a restore rather than at a review**, which is row 7's own warning about
its own rule.

---

## 8. Downgrade is three questions, and two are already answered

| Sense                    | Status                                                                                                                                     |
| ------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| **Suite downgrade**      | Closed by row 1. A carrier version selects the whole suite, every carrier authenticates its own version, and there is nothing to negotiate |
| **Product downgrade**    | **Not this row's, and it was wrong to file it here** — §2 closes the `rotate`/`retire` pair; TRD §14.7 carries the lapse state (`S0-7`)    |
| **Generation downgrade** | **Open, irreducibly, and bounded rather than closed** — §9                                                                                 |

**The middle one has a cryptographic answer that is smaller than it looks, and a carrier this row does not
supply.** A lapse and a deletion differ in exactly one artifact: the terminal record. §13.5's three lineage
states make a lapse _live but dormant_ and a deletion _retired_, and §14.4 already commits the terminal record
**before** anything is deleted. So the fail-closed direction is already the specified one — an interrupted
deletion leaves a retired lineage with its hosted content still present, which is honest and
recoverable-looking. **This row's contribution is to say that the ordering is the fail-closed property rather
than an implementation detail, and to give `kind` a negative.**

**What it is not is a lapse.** _Live but dormant_ names a state; naming a state is not carrying it, and this
protocol has no message that says a workspace is in one. §14.7 supplies the carrier — a signed retention mark on
a second axis, one clock created by whichever event stops synchronization, and a deletion ledger whose cause
decides whether the recovery anchor survives. **Retirement wins the race with a lapse in both orders**, by one
rule rather than an arbitration table: `cause` is set once, retirement may overwrite an entitlement cause, and
nothing overwrites retirement. That keeps this grammar at three kinds, which matters beyond tidiness — §3's
three-way rule, §2's wire theorem and the idempotency argument were all argued about three.

---

## 9. Where the guarantee stops, and it does not stop where the cryptography does

**A partitioned device keeps writing under the old generation, and an excluded credential can read those writes.**
The client switches generation on observing the committed outcome; a device that has not observed it has not
switched. §11.2 test 6 requires admitting "a genuine late-arriving old-epoch update from a still-authorized
offline device", so this is not a defect to be refused — it is the offline-first guarantee and the rotation
guarantee meeting.

**It cannot be closed without refusing to write while possibly stale**, which is PRD §2's local-first promise
inverted, and §7.1's rule that the local edit path has no network dependency. So it is bounded and stated:

- **The window is one device's propagation delay**, not the lifetime of the workspace.
- **§7.5's finalized head makes the exclusion legible to the excluded credential** — _the workspace stopped
  accepting your writes at position n_ — so it is not inferring anything from silence (§13.7, row 5).
- **The excluded credential still has to obtain the ciphertext**, and the finalization boundary is what refuses
  it. A hostile relay that serves it anyway is §11.2 test 6.
- **Row 9's residual is the same bound from the other side**: a hidden revocation is a hidden generation, so a
  stale head cannot come with current content.

**So the honest promise of a rotation is narrower than the obvious one, and the product owes the narrow version.**
Not _your workspace is now closed to that device_ — its history never was, and it holds those generations
already. **From the commit, content written by devices that have observed it is closed to that credential.** The
distinction is exactly one propagation delay wide and it is the only part a user could act on.

---

## 10. What it costs

| Cost             | Measured or bounded                                                                                | Against                                                        |
| ---------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Bundle           | **None new**                                                                                       | Ed25519 and SHA-256 are WebCrypto and row 1's                  |
| Key store        | One pending-intent record, present only during a transition                                        | Per slot                                                       |
| Service          | One signature per settled transition, and an at-most-once table keyed by `(lineage, kind, target)` | It already serializes successor commits (§13.5)                |
| Liveness         | **A client that cannot reach the service stays pending** and does not rebuild                      | Accepted, and §4 is why: rebuilding on a timeout is the attack |
| Rotation latency | Bounded below by one round trip that must complete                                                 | Off §12: rotation is not on the edit path                      |

---

## 11. What Stage 4 owes, and what is still open

**Owed by Stage 4, and none of it is Stage 1's.** No on-disk shape changes: the pending-intent record lives in the
key store, which Stage 1 creates, but nothing writes one until there is a service to submit to.

- **The at-most-once commit table** is the service's, and it is the one piece of server state this row requires.
  Its subject and retention belong in §16.1 and are added there.
- **The copy for a stuck pending transition**, which §4 makes a state a user can be in and §10 makes one they
  cannot shorten. It is row 13's two-texts problem again: honest about a rotation that has not completed, without
  implying compromise.
- **The narrow promise in §9** has to reach the interface, or the interface will say the wide one.

**Open, and offered to 3b rather than answered here.**

- **Whether the service should rate-limit or otherwise bound intent submission.** Row 14 §5 and row 12 both hand
  3b service behaviours; this is the third, and the three are one question about what the account service
  promises.
- **How long a pending intent may stay pending before the product says something**, which is a copy and support
  question with a cryptographic floor of _forever_ (§4). It is deliberately not a timeout.
- **Whether `replace-recovery`'s target counter needs to be service-assigned.** It is treated here as
  client-chosen and monotone, which is sufficient for at-most-once but leaves two devices able to race to counter
  1 with different keys — resolved by the same three-way rule, at the cost of one wasted keypair.

---

## 12. The vectors

`node scripts/generate-transition-vectors.mjs` writes them; `--check` fails if they are stale. The generator
verifies itself on every run: keypairs are checked half against half, every published vector is settled through
the real rule, every negative is asserted to fail, and the published must-fail list is compared against what was
actually asserted in both directions.

**Three kinds.**

The **intent vectors** pin all three kinds. The `rotate` and `retire` intents are published deliberately adjacent,
because §2's claim is only convincing as a diff.

The **outcome vectors** pin both verdicts, and the `superseded` one is the vector to read: it is the only answer
that licenses discarding a live key, and therefore the one an attacker would forge.

The **demonstrations** are behaviours that succeed and are meant to — row 6's way of publishing a residual. The
one that matters is `an-outcome-re-served-is-not-a-replay`: row 9's head assertion needed a nonce because a head
is a statement about a moving lineage, and `(lineage, kind, target)` names a pair reached once, so re-serving an
outcome forever is the truth rather than staleness. **Row 9 and this row reach opposite conclusions from the same
question, and the difference is whether the subject moves.**

The **negatives**, twenty, in three groups: the anchor (`fabricated-refusal`, `unsigned-outcome`), the ordering
(`outcome-from-an-older-epoch`), and sixteen fields across two bound lists, each isolated.

**The coverage audit refused three passes, and the third refusal is the interesting one.**

- Four intent negatives failed twice, because `settle` compares `kind`, `workspace`, `lineage` and `target`
  between the two messages. Fixed by supplying the matching outcome, re-signed — **row 12's fix, and the second
  row where it was needed**, which suggests a field read on both sides of a comparison is the ordinary case rather
  than an unusual one.
- `aad-only-outcome-committed-id` had an inner check on the verdict, which made it fail for a second reason.
  Removing it is the correction: `committed_id` is read from the record rather than recomputed, so eliding it from
  the signed message cannot change the verdict — **what changes is whether the signature refuses the edit at all**,
  and that is the property the negative is for.
- Then it was rescued by **two** fields, and the second one is a genuine trap. The substituted id was the rival
  rotation's, and the rival differs from the base intent in `payload_digest` alone — so eliding that one field
  makes the two ids equal and the negative passes for a reason unrelated to the signature. **A negative built from
  a near neighbour is isolated by the neighbourhood**, and the fix is to substitute an id that differs in two
  fields: the `retire` intent's.
